01

What a proof is for

A proof is something you can check without trusting its author.

Photo: Benjamin le Roux / Unsplash
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B04 / 40

Short section. The goal is one idea: a proof is something you can check without trusting its author. That asymmetry is what makes AI-generated proofs usable at all.

The key asymmetry

Finding a proof is hard. Checking one is easier.

Finding · search

Explore a huge space of ideas, constructions and dead ends. Can take decades — or thousands of machine hours.

Checking · verify

Follow each step and confirm it is valid. Can be done by someone — or something — that never had the idea.

Why it matters · trust

A proof is a certificate. You should not have to trust the author, human or machine, to accept it.

Find · two whole numbers above 1 whose product is 8,633

×
Give the class 30 seconds.

Check · someone hands you an answer

This gap lets machines generate expensive candidates that something cheaper and independent can check.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B05 / 40

Interactive: Let students try to factor 8,633 for 30 seconds, then press “Check 89 × 97”. Same lesson as sudoku: solving is hard, checking is quick.

Use a sudoku analogy if helpful: solving is hard, checking a filled grid is quick. In mathematics the gap can be enormous. This is the economic logic of AI proofs: let a machine spend huge effort generating candidates, then use a cheaper, independent process — a human referee or a proof checker — to accept or reject. If checking were as hard as finding, AI proofs would be nearly worthless.

Two kinds of proof text

Informal proofs and formal proofs

Informal (human prose)

Written for trained readers. Skips routine steps (“clearly…”). Errors can hide in the gaps. Easy to read, hard to check completely.

Formal (e.g., Lean)

Every step in a language a program can check, down to the axioms. A small trusted kernel accepts or rejects it. Hard to read, mechanically certain.

Autoformalization

Translating informal mathematics into formal code — the step AI has recently made fast.

Same claim, two ways
Claim. The sum of two even numbers is even.
Proof. Write a = 2m and b = 2n. Then a + b = 2(m + n), which is even. ∎
theorem even_add_even {a b : ℕ}
    (ha : Even a) (hb : Even b) : Even (a + b) :=
  ha.add hb   -- Mathlib lemma Even.add
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B06 / 40

Interactive: Toggle between the prose proof and the Lean version of the same fact.

Informal proofs are how mathematics has always been written: they skip routine steps and rely on a trained reader. Formal proofs spell out every step in a language a program can check. Most AI work now moves between the two: models write informal prose, and some systems translate it into Lean (autoformalization). Keep the trade-off in view: formal is mechanically certain, informal is readable.

Two purposes

Certainty is not the same as understanding

Certainty

Is the statement true? A checkable proof answers this — and machines are getting very good at it.

Understanding

Why is it true? What does it connect to? What new questions does it open? This is what mathematicians mainly value.

“The actual solving of these problems is only a proxy goal” for developing mathematical understanding and insight.

— Terence Tao, blog post, September 7, 2026
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B07 / 40

Tao's line from September 7 is the anchor: solving is a proxy goal; the real goal is understanding. Etingof's point (Quanta, Oct 5) is the cultural version: a theorem nobody reads does not enter mathematics as a living subject. Keep this tension in mind for Part 5 — machines are now very good at certainty and much less clearly good at producing understanding.

02

How machines prove

Fifty years of machine help — and what is new in 2025–26.

Photo: Florian Hirzinger – www.fh-ap.com / Wikimedia Commons
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B08 / 40

Machines have helped with proofs for fifty years. What is new in 2025–26 is that general reasoning models write the arguments themselves, and formal checkers can now keep up.

Not new: fifty years of machine help

Computers entered proofs long before chatbots

The 1976 argument — is a proof no human can check by hand really a proof? — is back, at far larger scale.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B09 / 40

Historical anchors, all well documented. Four Color Theorem: Appel and Haken, 1976, checked many map configurations by computer — controversial because no human could check every case. Robbins conjecture: proved by the automated prover EQP (William McCune) in 1996. Kepler conjecture: Hales's computer-assisted proof 1998; the Flyspeck project completed a formal proof in 2014. Gonthier's formal proof of the Four Color Theorem in Coq, 2005. The 1976 debate — is a proof nobody can read by hand really a proof? — is the same debate we are having now, at much larger scale.

Three engines

How AI produces mathematics today

1 · Reasoning models

Large language models trained to think at length write proofs in ordinary mathematical prose. Fast and flexible — but can skip or fudge hard steps.

2 · Formal provers

Systems that write proofs in Lean, where a small trusted program checks every step. Slow by hand; AI now writes them quickly.

3 · Search and construction

Programs that hunt for an explicit object — a counterexample, an algorithm, a configuration — and test it. Good at “find one that works”.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B10 / 40

These three engines are increasingly combined in one system. Engine 1 is what most people picture. Engine 2 is what makes results trustworthy at scale. Engine 3 is behind many of the counterexamples covered in the companion deck (unit-distance, Jacobian), and behind AlphaEvolve's records.

Engine 2 · Lean in one picture

A small program that refuses to be impressed

01

Statement

The claim, written precisely in Lean’s language.

02

Proof script

Step-by-step argument — now often written by AI.

03

Kernel

Small trusted program checks every step down to the axioms.

04

Revise

Errors go back to the model, which revises and tries again.

05

Accepted

Every step checks.

Blind spot

The kernel checks the proof against the statement you wrote — not against the statement you meant.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B12 / 40

Interactive: Step through: the error message is what turns a model’s guess into a loop.

Walk through the flow. The statement must be written in Lean's language; the proof is a script of steps; the kernel — a small program trusted by everyone — checks each step back to the axioms. If anything fails, Lean returns an error that a model can read and try to fix. That error message is what turns a model's guess into a loop. The one thing the kernel cannot judge is whether the statement you wrote is the one you meant (see slide 27).

“An extraordinary autoformalization achievement.”

— Kevin Buzzard, who began the human-led Lean formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 2024

Different job from Navier–Stokes: this checks a proof accepted since 1995. It creates certainty, not a new theorem.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B13 / 40

Source: Anthropic, 'Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem', Sep 4, 2026. An internal research model 'roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.1' running dozens of agents in a Claude Code-based setup, about 11 days largely autonomous, ~13 million lines of Lean (over five times the size of Mathlib), 29,500 intermediate theorems in the final proof, using only Lean's three standard axioms. It adapts pieces of Kevin Buzzard's Imperial College FLT project, which began in 2024. Buzzard reviewed it and called it an 'extraordinary autoformalization achievement'. Earlier: Math Inc's Gauss finished the strong Prime Number Theorem formalization in about 3 weeks (2025) after an 18-month human-led project. Note the difference from Navier–Stokes: FLT was already accepted (Wiles, 1995); this checks a known proof rather than producing a new theorem.

Engine 3 · search and construction

Sometimes the proof is an object you can test

AlphaEvolve · 2025

A way to multiply 4×4 complex matrices with 48 multiplications — beating a 1969 method.

Jacobian · Jul 2026

A counterexample in three dimensions refutes an 87-year-old conjecture (2D remains open).

Unit distance · May 2026

Infinitely many point sets with more unit distances than Erdős believed possible.

Multiplications needed for a 4×4 matrix product

Schoolbook4 × 4 × 464
Strassen, 1969applied twice: 7 × 749
AlphaEvolve, 2025complex-valued entries48

One fewer multiplication matters when the method is reused inside bigger products — and anyone can test it.

Why constructions spread first: checking an explicit object is easy, even when finding it was hard.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B14 / 40

A counterexample or construction is the easiest kind of result to verify: you just check the object. AlphaEvolve (DeepMind, May 2025): a procedure for multiplying 4×4 complex matrices using 48 scalar multiplications, beating Strassen's 1969 approach; on 50+ open problems it matched the best known answer ~75% of the time and improved ~20%. Jacobian conjecture (July 2026): Levent Alpöge posted a three-dimensional counterexample found with Claude, verified by independent mathematicians. Unit-distance (May 2026) is covered in detail in the companion deck — mention only.

The proving ground

Why obscure Erdős problems fell first

The catalogue

Erdős left hundreds of problems. As of Aug 3, 2026: 565 solved, 652 open (erdosproblems.com).

The long tail

Tao: AI’s scale suits the “long tail” of obscure problems — many turn out to have straightforward solutions.

Fast movement

Christmas 2025 to mid-January 2026: 15 problems moved to solved; 11 credited AI involvement.

Cautionary tale

Problem #333 was hailed as the first fully autonomous AI solution. What happened a few hours later?

Another user found it had been resolved in a 1977 paper by Erdős himself. A public problem list quickly becomes a benchmark — and a literature search becomes part of the proof.
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B15 / 40

Sources: Quanta, 'Why the legendary Erdős problems are falling to AI' (Aug 3, 2026): erdosproblems.com listed 565 solved and 652 open problems; the #333 episode — Kevin Barreto and Liam Price posted what they believed was the first fully autonomous AI solution on Christmas morning 2025, and hours later another user noted Erdős had resolved it in a 1977 paper; Barreto then urged 'greater focus on literature search'. TechCrunch (Jan 14, 2026): Tao suggested AI's scalability suits the 'long tail' of obscure Erdős problems, many with straightforward solutions; 15 problems moved from open to solved since Christmas, 11 crediting AI. Contrast: on Epoch's FrontierMath Erdős set of 68 significant open problems (Sep 1, 2026), the best public model solved 2.

Putting the engines together

The modern loop: generate, check, revise — at scale

Generate

Many agents propose ideas and write proof attempts.

→
Check

Another pass, code, or Lean tests every step.

→
Revise

Errors feed back; good pieces are merged and reused.

↺
Scale
×10,000

agents reportedly ran in parallel on the Navier–Stokes problem

The principle
Cheap checks

Expensive guessing is fine if checking is cheap and independent.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B16 / 40

This is the architecture behind the 2026 results: many agents generate attempts in prose; verifiers (another model pass, code execution, or Lean) check them; failures feed back. The September Navier–Stokes run reportedly used about 10,000 such agents in parallel. The design principle is the asymmetry from slide 5 — spend a lot on generation, rely on cheap, independent checking.

Activity · 3 minutes

Which check catches which error?

1A step says “clearly” — but it is actually falseAn invalid step fails in Lean; a careful referee may also catch it.
2The formal statement quietly proves an easier problem than the real oneOnly a person comparing the formal statement with the intended problem — Lean will happily accept a correct proof of the wrong statement.
3The “new” result was already published in a 1977 paperA literature search — exactly what happened with Erdős problem #333.
4A sign slip buried on page 40 of a long calculationLean or computer checking — the kind of slip humans miss in long computations.
Some flaws can be caught by more than one check. Is there one that only a human can catch?
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B17 / 40

Interactive: Pairs pick a check for each flaw, then press “Check our answers”.

Pairs match each flaw to the check that would catch it. Suggested answers: (1) Lean or a careful referee — an invalid step fails in Lean; a referee may or may not catch it. (2) Only a human comparing the formal statement with the intended problem — Lean will happily accept a correct proof of the wrong statement. (3) A literature search — e.g., Erdős problem #333 was claimed as an AI solution but turned out to be in a 1977 paper (Quanta, Aug 3, 2026). (4) Lean or computer checking — exactly the kind of slip humans miss in long computations. The lesson: no single check covers everything.

03

Case study: Navier–Stokes

The deepest claim of 2026, examined with the tools from Part 2.

Photo: Frankemann / Wikimedia Commons
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B18 / 40

The deepest claim of 2026, examined with the tools from Part 2. The companion deck introduced the announcement; here we go through the mathematics, the machine run, and each layer of checking.

The equations in words

Newton’s second law for every drop of fluid

∂u/∂t + (u·∇)u=−∇p+νΔu+f,∇·u = 0
Acceleration

How the velocity of each parcel changes — including being carried by the flow itself.

= Pressure

Fluid is pushed from high pressure toward low pressure.

+ Viscosity

Internal friction that smooths out sharp differences.

+ External force

Anything pushing from outside — a stirring paddle, gravity, a fan.

Incompressible

The fluid neither bunches up nor thins out (like water).

Used for weather, blood flow and aircraft design — yet a basic question about them stayed open for 90 years. Hover over a term.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B19 / 40

Interactive: Hover or click each term of the equation to light the matching card.

The Navier–Stokes equations are F = ma written for a continuous fluid. For each tiny parcel: its acceleration (including being carried along by the flow) equals the push from pressure differences, plus viscous friction (which smooths things out), plus any external force. Incompressibility says the fluid neither bunches up nor thins out. They describe weather, blood flow, aircraft wings — and since 1934 nobody could prove whether smooth solutions always stay smooth in 3D.

The question

Can a smooth flow “break” in finite time?

Start
Smooth

Velocity varies gently everywhere; total energy is finite.

Question
Blow-up?

Can some velocity become infinite after a finite time?

Stakes
$1 million

Clay Millennium Prize Problem since 2000; open since Leray (1934).

Real water is made of molecules. The question is about the equations — whether they can predict something infinite.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B20 / 40

Jean Leray (1934) built 'weak' solutions that always exist but might not be smooth, and asked whether singularities could form. The Clay Mathematics Institute made it a Millennium Prize Problem in 2000 with a $1 million prize. Only one of the seven Millennium problems (Poincaré) had been officially resolved. A singularity here means some velocity becomes infinite at a finite time even though everything started smooth with finite energy. Real fluids are made of molecules, so the result is about the equations, not about tap water — but it tells us the equations can behave in ways no one could pin down.

The official rules

Clay’s four doors — opening any one wins

Click a door.

A smooth external force is explicitly allowed for doors C and D — a forced blow-up is not a loophole.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B21 / 40

Interactive: Click each door. A and B are the regularity answers (no force); C and D are breakdown answers (smooth force allowed).

Fefferman's official problem statement offers four alternatives. (A) and (B) are the 'regularity' answers with no external force, on all of space or on a periodic box (torus). (C) and (D) are 'breakdown' answers, where a smooth, rapidly decaying external force IS allowed. OpenAI claims (C) and, as a corollary, (D). So a forced blow-up is not a loophole: it is one of the four officially accepted outcomes. What it does not settle is the unforced version, which many find more natural.

The road to blow-up

Ninety years of human work set the stage

“Without our work, without our method, they would not have been able to prove it.”

— Diego Córdoba (EFE, Sep 9)
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B22 / 40

Each step narrowed the gap. Hou–Luo 2013: strong numerical evidence that Euler (no viscosity) can blow up in a cylinder with a boundary. Tao 2016: blow-up for an 'averaged' Navier–Stokes, showing that standard energy methods alone cannot rule it out. Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa 2023: blow-up for forced Euler, but the force was not smooth enough for the Clay rules. DeepMind with Gómez-Serrano and Buckmaster 2025: neural networks found new families of unstable singularities. Buckmaster–Alpöge Aug 2026: smooth-forced blow-up for Euler, Boussinesq and porous media, heavily AI-assisted and checked in Lean (Tao blog, Sep 7). OpenAI Sep 8: forced Navier–Stokes. Córdoba: 'without our work, without our method, they would not have been able to prove it.'

The construction, in pictures

A spinning vortex that thins faster than it shortens

Shape
A swirling column collapsing toward a point.
Speed
Grows without bound as t → 1.
Energy
Total kinetic energy stays finite.
The force
A smooth, localized push supplies what the vortex cannot.

Schematic with illustrative exponents — not the paper’s exact profile

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B23 / 40

Interactive: Drag time toward 1: the column narrows much faster than it shortens, peak speed shoots up, energy stays flat.

Described from OpenAI's paper and blog: an axisymmetric vortex (symmetric around an axis), spinning like a top, concentrates toward a point. It narrows radially faster than it shortens along its axis — 'stretching like spaghetti'. Swirl and axial speeds grow like (1 − t)^(−1/2 − h) as t approaches 1, while total kinetic energy stays bounded. The leading vortex leaves leftover stresses; oscillating 'pulses' and successive corrections are arranged so that what remains can be supplied by a smooth, compactly supported external force. That is why the result is a forced blow-up.

The claimed theorem

Theorem 1.1, in plain English

For any amount of viscosity, there is a smooth, localized force such that a fluid starting completely at rest stays smooth for a while — and then, at a finite time, its velocity becomes infinite while its total energy stays finite.

Paper

“Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes” — about 166 pages, author listed only as “OpenAI”.

Formal code

Lean files public on GitHub (openai/NavierStokesAndEuler).

Prize

“We do not intend to claim the Millennium Prize for this result.” — OpenAI

Announced September 8, 2026. Still under review — see the verification ladder.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B24 / 40

From the paper 'Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes' (OpenAI, Sep 8, 2026, about 166 pages, credited to 'OpenAI' with no individual authors). For every viscosity ν > 0 there exist a smooth, compactly supported force f and zero initial velocity such that the solution is smooth up to time 1, stays in a fixed bounded region, keeps finite energy, and yet its maximum velocity is unbounded as t approaches 1. Corollary: the same on the periodic box (door D). The repository github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler holds the Lean formalization (also covering an unforced Euler blow-up claim).

Lost in translation?

A green Lean check is not the end of the story

The critique (Oct 6)

A preprint argues the Lean proof “does not correspond” to the 166-page written proof — so a passing Lean check would not confirm the written argument.

Its own status

Posted one day before this lecture; not peer-reviewed. It may be right, partly right, or wrong.

The lasting lesson

A computer can certify a proof of a statement. Only people can certify that it is the statement we care about.

Bastounis, Circelli & Hansen, “Navier–Stokes lost in translation,” arXiv:2610.08144 (Oct 6, 2026).

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B27 / 40

Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen, 'Navier-Stokes lost in translation: Why Lean verification of AI autoformalisation does not guarantee correct natural language proofs', arXiv 2610.08144, submitted Oct 6, 2026. Their claim: 'the formalised Lean proof does not correspond to the NL proof.' Present this carefully: it is a one-day-old, unreviewed critique; it may be right, partly right, or wrong. The general lesson does not depend on who wins: a machine check certifies a formal statement, and humans must still confirm that statement and its proof match the mathematics everyone means.

Whose proof is it?

Provenance became part of the mathematics

Buckmaster & Alpöge

Smooth-forced Euler blow-up, Lean-checked in August 2026, heavily AI-assisted; posted hours before OpenAI.

Their concern

That word of their work — or Codex usage data — reached OpenAI’s system.

OpenAI’s response

Its investigation found Buckmaster’s prompts “could not have influenced the system”; it credits them for forced Euler.

The deeper issue

When AI and humans work on the same problem with shared tools, who contributed what?

Accounts of private conversations are contested and have not been independently verified.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B28 / 40

Keep this neutral — the facts are disputed. Tristan Buckmaster (NYU Courant) and Levent Alpöge (an Anthropic employee; he says the collaboration was personal) had Lean-verified smooth-forced blow-up results for Euler, Boussinesq and porous media from mid-August, using Claude, Codex and later GPT models, and posted about 12 hours before OpenAI. Buckmaster alleged word of their work reached OpenAI and that his Codex sessions might have informed it. OpenAI says its researchers and agents did not see their work, said on Sep 10 that an investigation found his Codex prompts 'could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training', recognized their priority on forced Euler, and says its own Euler result is unforced. Not resolved as of early October.

What is settled — and what is not

Read the scope before the headline

If it holds

A smooth flow pushed by a smooth, localized force can develop infinite velocity in finite time. That opens Clay’s door C (and D).

Still open

Can it happen with no external force at all? Tao thinks the forcing may eventually be removable — but nobody has shown it.

Still pending

Independent expert verification, journal publication, and the Clay Institute’s own process.

“I was thrilled that the problem was solved.”

— Charles Fefferman, author of the official Clay problem statement (Quanta, Sep 8)
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B29 / 40

If the claim holds, door C is opened under Clay's wording. Still open: blow-up or regularity with NO external force — Tao (Sep 7) thinks the Buckmaster–Alpöge methods might eventually work 'without the forcing term'. Still open: physical relevance, since real fluids are molecular. Still pending: independent verification, publication, and Clay's process. Fefferman (Quanta): 'I was thrilled that the problem was solved.' Tsimerman (Heidelberg): 'solving Navier-Stokes feels pretty definitive.'

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B32 / 40

Family numbers and titles are as listed in the README; none of these had independent confirmation as of Oct 7. 017 'The irrationality exponent of π' — how well π can be approximated by fractions. 197 'Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture in characteristic two' — an algebra question from the 1970s. 287 'Isomorphism of free group factors' — a famous operator-algebra question. The README lists two exceptions to its standard procedure: a zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function (human-edited for readability) and the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties (a special case of a different Millennium problem). Some commentators have questioned whether others are as long-standing as described, or already in the literature — a known failure mode (October 2025 Erdős episode).

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B33 / 40

AGMAI (Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI, hosted at IAS; members Charles, De Lellis, Gowers, Hairer, Srivastava, Tillmann, Vakil, Witten, Wood) issued guidelines on Sep 29 based on 600+ community responses: deposit results in repositories 'not controlled by any AI lab'; disclose model name, prompts, chain of thought, time and cost; check and cite literature; formalize in Lean where possible; report failures and how problems were chosen; 'refrain from treating the release of mathematical results as marketing vehicles'. My reading of the Oct 6 release against that list is shown; AGMAI itself said its role 'is not an endorsement' and that the release is 'the beginning, not the completion, of the process of human understanding'.

Who reads 722 papers?

Mathematics is a human activity — at least so far

The bottleneck

Generating a paper now takes hours of compute. Understanding and checking one still takes a specialist days to months.

System strain

Quanta reports arXiv now limits authors to two submissions a month, and some mathematicians no longer post open conjectures.

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B35 / 40

Pairs build a minimum list, then compare with the AGMAI scorecard on slide 33. Good answers include: a human (or named team) who takes responsibility; the exact model and prompts; a formal statement plus a human check that it matches; a literature search; independent referees; and a statement of what was NOT shown (e.g., forced vs unforced). Ask: would your list differ if the same paper came from a famous human mathematician? Why or why not?

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B37 / 40

Fields Medalists' declaration 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics' (mathandai.org, Sep 11; 25 initial signatories, 28 listed now, including Tao, Scholze, Bhargava, Viazovska, Hairer, Maynard). Gowers explained on Sep 17 why he did not sign: he does not fully share the view that understanding should take priority over problem-solving, and worries most about fewer people choosing PhDs. Scholze at the Heidelberg Laureate Forum: 'some kind of PR stunt'. Williamson: 'OpenAI behaved extremely poorly'. Tsimerman: 'solving Navier-Stokes feels pretty definitive'. Tao (Sep 8) warned of good open problems being mined in a non-renewable way. Society statements: AMS congratulated both groups; EMS called the model being internal and inaccessible 'a major problem'; LMS: 'the goal remains human understanding'.

A new division of labor

What machines now do — and what people still decide

Search huge spaces of ideasMachines now do this — fast and at scale.
Choose which questions matterStill a human job, as every source in this lecture kept saying.
Write long proof attemptsMachines now do this — fast and at scale.
Judge what a formal statement meansStill a human job, as every source in this lecture kept saying.
Check every step formallyMachines now do this — fast and at scale.
Explain why something is trueStill a human job, as every source in this lecture kept saying.
Translate known proofs into LeanMachines now do this — fast and at scale.
Set the rules for credit and accessStill a human job, as every source in this lecture kept saying.

Tao: identifying a promising problem is “the scarce and precious resource.”

AI × Mathematics · Week 9B38 / 40

Interactive: Read each task aloud; the class calls Machines or People before you click.

This is a synthesis, not a prediction. Machines have become strong at search, at writing and checking long arguments, and at formalization. The human jobs that remain central are the ones every source in this lecture kept returning to: choosing which questions matter (Tao: identifying a promising problem is 'the scarce and precious resource'), judging whether a formal statement means what we intend, explaining why something is true, and deciding norms of credit and access.

Exit ticket · 2 minutes

Claimed, checked, or accepted?

Claimed

Someone says it is true.

Checked

An independent process confirmed it.

Accepted

The community has absorbed it.

Result 1Fermat’s Last Theorem, fully machine-checked in Lean (Sep 4)Checked: machine-verified (and reviewed by Buzzard) — of a theorem already accepted since 1995.
Result 2Erdős unit-distance conjecture disproved by an AI model (May 20)Checked by external mathematicians with a companion paper; well on the way to accepted.
Result 3Forced Navier–Stokes blow-up claimed by OpenAI (Sep 8)Claimed: a public Lean check whose match to the written proof is contested; not yet accepted.
Place each result, then write one sentence explaining why.
AI × Mathematics · Week 9B39 / 40

Each student places the three results on the three-word scale and writes one sentence of justification. Suggested placement as of Oct 7: Fermat formalization — checked (machine-verified, reviewed by Buzzard) of an already-accepted theorem. Unit-distance disproof — checked by external mathematicians with a companion paper; well on the way to accepted (Tsimerman: 'I would accept it for any journal without hesitation'). Navier–Stokes — claimed, with a public Lean check whose correspondence to the written proof is contested; not yet accepted. The point is that these three words mean different things, and headlines usually blur them.
